fact_en:
How do electric and magnetic fields keep each other going in a wave?

In an electromagnetic wave, a changing electric field creates a magnetic field, and the changing magnetic field creates the electric field again—so they keep each other going!
fact_bis:
Giunsa pagpadayon sa usag usa ang electric field ug magnetic field sa usa ka wave?

Sa electromagnetic wave, ang nag-usab nga electric field maghimo og magnetic field, ug ang nag-usab nga magnetic field maghimo pag-usab sa electric field—mao nga sila magpadayon sa usag usa!

findings.note: Title_bis "Mga Patlang sa EM" — patlang is a GAP/BLANK/interval, not a field, so the title reads "EM gaps" for "EM Fields". The body uses "electric field"/"magnetic field" correctly, and patlang appears in no other card in the whole 337-batch corpus (other cards use "Magnetic Field"/"Magnetikong Field").

fact_en:
Why is a bird's egg shell so hard?

The hard shell protects the growing chick inside from harm until it is ready to hatch!
fact_bis:
Ngano nga gahi ang bagol sa itlog sa langgam?

Giprotektahan sa gahi nga bagol ang nagtubo nga piso sa sulod gikan sa kadaot hangtod mapusa kini!

findings.note: Title_bis "Kabibi sa Itlog" — kabibi is a CLAM/bivalve, not an egg shell, and the card never supplies a correct word: the body says "bagol sa itlog" (bagol = coconut shell/skull). All 11 other eggshell cards in the corpus use "panit sa itlog" or "kabhang sa itlog"; kabibi is reserved there for nautilus/seashells.

fact_en: A collapsible steering column is designed to shorten in a frontal crash! This device does less harm to the driver's chest.
fact_bis: Ang collapsible steering column gidisenyo aron mub-an sa frontal crash! Kini usa ka gamit nga nagpaliti sa kadaot sa manibela sa dughan sa driver.

findings.note: Body: "Kini usa ka gamit nga nagpaliti sa kadaot sa manibela sa dughan sa driver." English is "This device does less harm to the driver's chest." In Cebuano palit/paliti = TO BUY (the Tagalog-shaped nagpapaliit 'makes smaller' does not exist here), so the sentence reads as the device 'buying' the steering wheel's harm to the driver's chest — the whole point (LESS harm) is gone, and it can even read as the device causing the chest harm. The rest of the card does not restore it: the first sentence only says the column is designed to shorten ("gidisenyo aron mub-an") in a frontal crash and never states any reduction of injury, so the card's single safety fact is unrecoverable.

fact_en:
How do continents and oceans move around the Earth?

The lithosphere is broken into large plates that move in different directions, carrying continents and oceans with them!
fact_bis:
Unsaon paglihok sa mga kontinente ug kadagatan sa tibuok kalibotan?

Ang lithosphere nabahin ngadto sa dagkong mga plates nga naglihok sa lain-laing direksyon, dala ang mga kontinente ug kadagatan!

findings.note: Title reads "Plato sa Litospera" — plato in Cebuano is a dinner plate, not a tectonic plate (plaka / the English 'plates'). A child reading only the title gets "the lithosphere's dinner plate". The card's OWN body uses the correct term ("nabahin ngadto sa dagkong mga plates"), and the terms list carries "plaka", so the title is the outlier. Title fact (the lithosphere is split into plates) is not recoverable from the title itself.

fact_en: Scientists use a small bubble level to check if the table is perfectly level, so the block won't slide on its own before pulling!
fact_bis: Naggamit ang mga scientist ug gamay nga bubble level aron masiguro nga patas ang table, mao nga dili mopalta ang block sa dili pa birahon!

findings.note: EN: "...so the block won't slide on its own before pulling." BIS: "...mao nga dili mopalta ang block sa dili pa birahon." Cebuano/Spanish-derived `palta` (falta) = to be absent / missing / lacking; it has no motion sense. The whole reason for levelling the table -- that an unlevel table lets the block slide by itself -- becomes "so the block won't go missing before it is pulled", and nothing else on the card restores "slide" (body says only `patas ang table`, terms carry `kuskos`/`patag` but never a sliding verb). Correct would be modalin-as / modahili. Title `Parehas nga Lamesa` (= "same table") also does not carry "level", so the causal fact is unrecoverable from the Cebuano alone.

fact_en:
How can we check if a jar truly has no carbon dioxide?

We use limewater! It turns milky when carbon dioxide is present, so it checks if the jar is truly empty of it.
fact_bis:
Unsaon nato pagsiguro nga ang garapon tinuod nga walay carbon dioxide?

Naggamit kita og limewater! Mahimong gatas kini kon adunay carbon dioxide, mao nga masusi niini kung ang garapon tinuod nga walay carbon dioxide.

findings.note: title_bis "Tubig-dayap CO2 Test" for "Limewater CO2 Test": dayap is the citrus lime fruit (the corpus glosses it that way at ffct-04304, 'mokaon og dayap (lime)'), not calcium hydroxide. The body uses the English word limewater but never defines it, so the title's wrong substance is never corrected — a child would think the CO2 test uses citrus-lime water. 19 other limewater cards keep 'limewater'; only this title and ffct-39805 say Tubig-dayap. The error is also baked into this card's terms array.

fact_en:
What does it mean when displacement is a vector?

It means it includes both how far a point moved and its direction, like moving '5 centimeters west'!
fact_bis:
Unsay pasabot nga ang displacement usa ka vector?

Nagpasabot nga apil niini kung unsa kalayo milihok ang punto ug ang direksyon niini, sama sa '5 centimeters paingon sa kasadpan'!

findings.note: title_bis "Paglihok sa Plato" for "Plate Displacement": plato = dinner plate, not a tectonic plate. The body never mentions a plate at all (it only explains displacement as a vector, '5 centimeters paingon sa kasadpan'), so nothing in the card corrects it. Corpus-wide, all 186 tectonic-plate cards use plate/plates/plaka — including ffct-39677 in this same batch ("Pilipinas nga Plate") — never plato.

fact_en:
What is limewater made of, and when does it change?

Limewater is a clear solution of calcium hydroxide in water. It stays clear until carbon dioxide gas reacts with it!
fact_bis:
Unsa ang limewater ug kanus-a kini magbag-o?

Ang limewater kay klaro nga solusyon sa calcium hydroxide sa tubig. Magpabilin kini nga klaro hangtod mo-react ang carbon dioxide gas!

findings.note: title_bis renders "Limewater" as "Tubig-dayap" = water of DAYAP, the citrus lime fruit. Chemical lime is apog (the same corpus uses apog for limestone/lime and dayap only for the citrus fruit), so the title names a different substance — a fruit drink — than the calcium hydroxide solution the card is about. The card's own body keeps the correct word ("Ang limewater kay klaro nga solusyon sa calcium hydroxide sa tubig"), and every other limewater card in this batch (ffct-39700/39701/39706/39710/39712/39804) leaves it as "limewater", so the title is the outlier. Nothing in the Cebuano ever says it is not made from dayap, leaving a child to believe limewater is citrus-lime water.

fact_en:
Why does honey pour so slowly?

Its particles attract each other more strongly than water particles, making it thick and viscous!
fact_bis:
Nganong hinay mobuhagay ang honey?

Mas kusog nga magtinabangay ang mga particle niini kaysa sa tubig, mao nga kini baga o viscous!

findings.note: Body: "Mas kusog nga magtinabangay ang mga particle niini kaysa sa tubig" for EN "Its particles attract each other more strongly than water particles". Cebuano magtinabangay (root tabang) = to HELP ONE ANOTHER / cooperate, never physical attraction; attraction is magdinanihay / nagbirahay / kusog nga pagdani sa usag usa. The mechanism the card exists to teach — inter-particle attraction — appears nowhere else in the Cebuano (no dani/bira anywhere in bis or title_bis), so a child reading only the Cebuano learns honey is viscous because its particles "help each other", and cannot answer why honey pours slowly. Title_bis (Lagkit sa Dugos) is fine; the defect is the verb in the answer.
